COPYRIGHT TERMINATION RIGHT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Jordan Morgan

DECLARATION
This information sheet describes the federal statutory termination right created by 17 U.S.C. § 203, and, where a grant predates the current copyright statute, the related pathway in 17 U.S.C. § 304(c) and (d) — the right that lets an individual author, or certain statutorily defined successors, terminate a copyright transfer or license decades after it was made, regardless of what the transfer agreement itself says. It is prepared with reference to a grant by Jordan Alex Lee to Jordan Morgan covering Riverbend (novel), executed on or about June 1, 2010, for use as background information about how the federal termination-of-transfer provisions generally operate. This sheet does not itself terminate any grant, does not constitute or substitute for an advance notice of termination under 17 U.S.C. § 203 or § 304, and does not determine whether Jordan Alex Lee, Jordan Morgan, or any grant between them is in fact eligible for termination — eligibility depends on facts (including who executed the grant, when, and whether the underlying work was made for hire) that this sheet does not resolve. Copyright is exclusively a matter of federal law; this sheet describes no California-specific rule.

THE TERMINATION RIGHT AND ITS OVERRIDE OF CONTRARY AGREEMENTS
Federal copyright law lets an author terminate a grant — an exclusive or nonexclusive transfer or license of copyright, or of any right under a copyright — that the author executed on or after January 1, 1978, other than by will. This termination right exists notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, including an agreement to make a will or to make a future grant, so a waiver of the termination right written into the original transfer agreement does not by itself prevent termination. This is a rule of federal law only; copyright is exclusively federal, and this termination right is not a feature of California law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "In the case of any work other than a work made for hire, the exclusive or nonexclusive grant of a transfer or license of copyright or of any right under a copyright, executed by the author on or after January 1, 1978, otherwise than by will, is subject to termination under the following conditions:"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers and licenses granted by the author — conditions (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  "Termination of the grant may be effected notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary, including an agreement to make a will or to make any future grant."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(5) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers — override of contrary agreements (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  Known gap: The statute's override language is quoted from 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(5); the identical override rule also appears, independently, in 17 U.S.C. § 304(c)(5), which governs a related but separate termination pathway for grants executed before 1978 (addressed elsewhere in this document). This clause states the general contours of the right — who specifically may exercise it, exactly when, and how — without addressing eligibility for a particular grant, which depends on facts such as who executed the grant, when, and whether the work is a work made for hire.

THE WORK-MADE-FOR-HIRE EXCEPTION
The termination right does not apply to a work made for hire. This exception is written directly into the statute's own conditions for termination, both for grants executed on or after January 1, 1978 and, separately, for the related pre-1978 termination pathway for renewal-term grants. A work made for hire is, by definition elsewhere in the Copyright Act, typically either work created by an employee within the scope of employment, or one of several specifically enumerated categories of specially ordered or commissioned work for which the parties have signed a written work-for-hire agreement — a status this sheet does not itself determine for any particular work.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "In the case of any work other than a work made for hire, the exclusive or nonexclusive grant of a transfer or license of copyright or of any right under a copyright, executed by the author on or after January 1, 1978, otherwise than by will, is subject to termination under the following conditions:"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers — work-made-for-hire exclusion (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  "In the case of any copyright subsisting in either its first or renewal term on January 1, 1978, other than a copyright in a work made for hire, the exclusive or nonexclusive grant of a transfer or license of the renewal copyright or any right under it, executed before January 1, 1978, by any of the persons designated by subsection (a)(1)(C) of this section, otherwise than by will, is subject to termination under the following conditions:"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 304(c) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers covering extended renewal term — work-made-for-hire exclusion (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/304)
  Known gap: The two citations below are drawn from two independent statutory sections — 17 U.S.C. § 203 (grants executed on or after January 1, 1978) and § 304(c) (pre-1978 renewal-term grants) — each of which independently excludes a work made for hire from its own termination right. Neither citation itself defines "work made for hire"; that definition appears in 17 U.S.C. § 101 and is addressed separately by this project's Copyright Assignment Agreement document, not reproduced or re-verified here.

WHO MAY EXERCISE THE RIGHT — AUTHOR AND STATUTORY HEIRS
Where a single author executed the grant, that author may effect termination, or, if the author has died, termination may be effected by whoever under the statute's ownership rules owns and is entitled to exercise more than one-half of that author's termination interest. Where an author has died, the statute distributes that author's termination interest among specific classes of survivors in a fixed order: the surviving spouse owns the entire interest unless the author also left surviving children or grandchildren, in which case the spouse owns one-half and the children (or, per stirpes, the surviving children of a deceased child) own the balance. This ownership scheme is not a general default for who inherits a decedent's property generally — it is a termination-interest allocation rule specific to this statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "In the case of a grant executed by one author, termination of the grant may be effected by that author or, if the author is dead, by the person or persons who, under clause (2) of this subsection, own and are entitled to exercise a total of more than one-half of that author’s termination interest."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers — who may terminate a single-author grant (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  "The widow or widower owns the author’s entire termination interest unless there are any surviving children or grandchildren of the author, in which case the widow or widower owns one-half of the author’s interest."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(2)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers — surviving spouse's share of a deceased author's termination interest (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  Known gap: Both citations below are subsections of the same statutory provision, 17 U.S.C. § 203(a) (clauses (1) and (2)); they are not independent sources of each other. Independent confirmation instead comes from a separate section: 17 U.S.C. § 304(c)(2)(A), governing the different pre-1978 termination pathway, uses identical operative language for the same spousal-share rule, which corroborates that this is the general statutory ownership formula rather than an artifact particular to § 203. This clause does not address the further per-stirpes subdivision among grandchildren, the rule for when no spouse, children, or grandchildren survive, or the joint-work rule requiring majority action among multiple living co-authors, all of which the statute also addresses in more granular detail than reproduced here.

THE TERMINATION WINDOW — POST-1978 GRANTS AND THE SEPARATE PRE-1978 PATHWAY
For a grant executed on or after January 1, 1978, termination may be effected at any time during a five-year window that begins at the end of thirty-five years from the date the grant was executed — or, if the grant covers the right of publication, the window instead begins at the earlier of thirty-five years from the date of publication under the grant or forty years from the date of execution. A separate, older pathway applies to a grant of renewal-term rights executed before January 1, 1978: there, the five-year termination window begins at the end of fifty-six years from the date copyright was originally secured (or January 1, 1978, whichever is later). Because a 1998 statutory amendment lengthened copyright's term, the statute also created a second, later five-year window — beginning at the end of seventy-five years from the date copyright was originally secured — for cases where the fifty-six-year-based termination right had already expired unused by the time that 1998 amendment took effect.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Termination of the grant may be effected at any time during a period of five years beginning at the end of thirty-five years from the date of execution of the grant; or, if the grant covers the right of publication of the work, the period begins at the end of thirty-five years from the date of publication of the work under the grant or at the end of forty years from the date of execution of the grant, whichever term ends earlier."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers — timing for post-1978 grants (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  "Termination of the grant may be effected at any time during a period of five years beginning at the end of fifty-six years from the date copyright was originally secured, or beginning on January 1, 1978, whichever is later."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 304(c)(3) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers covering extended renewal term — timing (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/304)
  "Termination of the grant may be effected at any time during a period of 5 years beginning at the end of 75 years from the date copyright was originally secured."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 304(d)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination rights that had expired before the Sonny Bono Copyright Term Extension Act — the later 75-year window (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/304)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two independent statutory sections: 17 U.S.C. § 203 (grants executed on or after January 1, 1978) and § 304(c)/(d) (grants executed before January 1, 1978, covering renewal-term rights). Within § 304, subsection (c)(3) and subsection (d)(2) are subdivisions of the same section and are not independent of each other; § 304(d)'s later window is available only where no termination was made under § 304(c) and only for copyrights originally secured in a specific historical date range, a further condition this clause does not restate in full. This clause states timing rules only; it does not address the separate two-to-ten-year advance notice requirement (addressed in another clause of this document) or resolve, for any specific grant, which of these windows (if any) applies.

NOTICE TIMING, CONTENT, AND RECORDATION
To exercise the termination right, an advance written notice must be served on the grantee or the grantee's successor in title, stating an effective termination date that falls within the applicable five-year window; the notice itself must be served not less than two nor more than ten years before that stated effective date. A copy of the notice must be recorded with the U.S. Copyright Office before the effective date of termination as a condition to the termination actually taking effect. The statute delegates the notice's required form, content, and manner of service to regulations the Register of Copyrights is directed to prescribe. The Copyright Office's own regulation implementing that delegation confirms it covers notices under both termination pathways — 17 U.S.C. § 203 and § 304(c)/(d) — states that the Office does not provide a printed form for this purpose, and requires that a notice under § 203 clearly identify, among other things, a statement that the termination is made under § 203, the grantee's name and address for service, the date of execution of the grant (and, if applicable, date of publication), the work's title and the author's name, a statement identifying the grant being terminated, and the stated effective date of termination.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "The notice shall comply, in form, content, and manner of service, with requirements that the Register of Copyrights shall prescribe by regulation."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(4)(B) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, termination of transfers — delegation of notice form/content/service rules to regulation (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  "This section covers notices of termination of transfers and licenses under 17 U.S.C. 203, 304(c), and 304(d)."
  — 37 C.F.R. § 201.10 (eCFR, current), Code of Federal Regulations, notices of termination of transfers and licenses (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-37/chapter-II/subchapter-B/part-201/section-201.10)
  "A notice of termination of an exclusive or nonexclusive grant of a transfer or license of copyright or of any right under a copyright, executed by the author on or after January 1, 1978, under 17 U.S.C. 203, must include a clear identification of each of the following:"
  — 37 C.F.R. § 201.10(b)(2) (eCFR, current), Code of Federal Regulations, required contents of a § 203 notice of termination (https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-37/chapter-II/subchapter-B/part-201/section-201.10)
  Known gap: The statutory citation (17 U.S.C. § 203(a)(4)(B)) and the regulatory citation (37 C.F.R. § 201.10) are independent sources of each other — one is enacted statute, the other is the U.S. Copyright Office's own implementing regulation issued under the statute's delegation of rulemaking authority. This clause summarizes only the § 203-specific content list in 37 C.F.R. § 201.10(b)(2); the regulation's content requirements for a § 304(c)/(d) notice differ somewhat and are not restated here, nor is the regulation's separate treatment of permitted service methods, harmless-error rules, or the mechanics of Copyright Office recordation once a notice has been served.

EFFECT OF A COMPLETED TERMINATION
Once termination takes effect, all rights under the Copyright Act that were covered by the terminated grant revert to the author, authors, or other persons who owned termination interests — including anyone who did not personally join in signing the notice of termination but was entitled to. Reversion is not absolute, however: a derivative work already prepared under the grant's authority before termination may continue to be used under the terms of the original grant even after termination, though this carve-out does not extend to preparing any new derivative works after termination. Separately, once rights revert, the statute restricts who may make a further grant of those same rights and generally requires that any further grant be made only after termination's effective date, subject to a narrow first-refusal-style exception for the original grantee.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-03]
  "Upon the effective date of termination, all rights under this title that were covered by the terminated grants revert to the author, authors, and other persons owning termination interests under clauses (1) and (2) of subsection (a), including those owners who did not join in signing the notice of termination under clause (4) of subsection (a), but with the following limitations:"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, effect of termination — reversion of rights (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  "A derivative work prepared under authority of the grant before its termination may continue to be utilized under the terms of the grant after its termination, but this privilege does not extend to the preparation after the termination of other derivative works based upon the copyrighted work covered by the terminated grant."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 203(b)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, effect of termination — derivative works prepared before termination (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/203)
  Known gap: The reversion rule (17 U.S.C. § 203(b)) and the specific derivative-work carve-out (§ 203(b)(1)) are drawn from the same statutory subsection and are not independent of each other. Independent confirmation of the derivative-work carve-out specifically comes from a separate section, § 304(c)(6)(A), governing the different pre-1978 termination pathway, which uses identical operative language. This clause does not restate the further-grant restrictions of § 203(b)(3)-(4) in full, including their own numerosity and timing requirements.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — COPYRIGHT TERMINATION RIGHT INFORMATION SHEET
The undersigned acknowledges reviewing this information sheet regarding the federal statutory termination right under 17 U.S.C. § 203 and, where applicable, § 304(c)/(d), in connection with a grant between Jordan Alex Lee and Jordan Morgan covering Riverbend (novel) executed on or about June 1, 2010.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature: _________________________

Jordan Alex Lee

[This information sheet is educational only. It is not an advance notice of termination, does not itself terminate any grant or license, and does not substitute for the notice, service, and Copyright Office recordation steps that federal law requires to actually effect a termination.]
